--- title: Publication workflow and review queue subtitle: A single, issue-to-review record for manuscript development --- This page is the working index for publication development. Each task is tracked like a small issue: it begins with an objective and guardrails, records the decisions and artifacts produced while it is open, and ends either in a reviewable manuscript product or a completed analytical record. The manuscript is developed backwards from the results displays: **figures and tables → results → methods → discussion → introduction → abstract → title**. This order adapts the “write backwards” approach described by [Montagnes, Montagnes, and Yang (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10077155/). ## How to use this queue Each task has a short proposal below it before any work is done. Review and edit that proposal, then move the task through this sequence: **Direction for review → Approved to execute → In progress → Pending review → Accepted (or Revision requested) → Complete.** “Queued” means the task is deliberately decomposed and ready to be proposed; it is not yet authorized for execution. “Completed — analytical record” means the reproducible work is preserved, while a decision explicitly marked provisional still awaits scientific review. Page targets are working allocations for the main manuscript, not a journal requirement. ## Task register This register is both the review checklist and the table of contents for the task cards. Results displays and their captions come first; each corresponding Results narrative follows only after its display is accepted. Methods then document the accepted results, followed by Discussion, Introduction, Abstract, and Title. | Order | Task | Status | Proposed target | |---:|---|---|---| | 0 | [F-01 — fuel-component preparation ### F-01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration {#f-01} **Status: Completed — analytical record.** #### Original objective and guardrails Create publication-only fuel components that preserve the thesis analyses while making the pre- and post-PCT data usable as distinct reference phases. Retain the fixed experimental-design random-intercept structure; record every model candidate and diagnostic; do not treat an AIC leader as a selected model. - Thesis notebooks, raw data, and thesis-era `.rda` objects remain unchanged. - Pre-PCT litter and duff are separated using the Finney–Martin model-3 forest-floor partition; post-PCT litter and duff are deliberately omitted because their boundary is not currently defensible. - Woody and herbaceous vegetation are separate in both phases. - The primary PCT contrast is matched-transect pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation—an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not a direct slash-load measurement. #### Decisions made | Decision area | Recorded decision | Why it matters for the publication display | |---|---|---| | Reporting phases | Show pre- and post-PCT values as distinct phases. | Avoids treating the contrast as automatically causal. | | Forest floor | Report modeled litter and duff only before PCT. | Prevents a misleading post-PCT forest-floor estimate. | | Vegetation | Keep woody and herbaceous components separate. | Allows the PCT-related standing-woody change to remain visible. | | PCT estimand | Use matched pre minus post woody standing vegetation. | Clearly labels the management contrast and its limitation. | | Model selection | Preserve all candidates; leaders are provisional pending scientific review. | Keeps model choice auditable instead of hiding it in a final table. | #### Rendered component dictionary The generated dictionary below is rendered from the publication artifact, so the displayed definitions and the downloadable record remain aligned. ::: {#tbl-fuel-component-dictionary .cell tbl-cap='Publication fuel-component dictionary generated by F-01.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Its position in the register is an organizational sequence, not a required execution order relative to R-D02 or R-D03. The [prediction and interpretation review](#rd04-inference-review) below now compares the thesis and R-D04 estimands, demonstrates both prediction implementations, and records the Methods wording. The figure now uses random-effect-integrated mean loads throughout and the joint woody phase model for the displayed pre-minus-post mean change. The completed display and its model assumptions are recorded below. #### Objective Produce a compact, reviewable full-inventory figure (and caption) from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. Use nine panels: paired pre-/ post-PCT estimates for 1-, 10-, 100-, and 1,000-hour fuels plus woody and herbaceous vegetation; pre-PCT-only panels for litter and duff; and a separate matched woody-vegetation-difference panel (pre-PCT minus post-PCT). The figure must retain uncertainty, retained-overstory treatment context, and the qualified interpretation of the vegetation-difference estimand. #### Constraints and starting material - Use the saved fitted models identified as AIC leaders in the F-01 model-selection register. Their diagnostic/scientific review remains visible through the figure-review decision rather than blocking draft generation. - Integrate over all fitted random effects for a consistent mean-load interpretation, with equal study-site weights. Derive woody mean change from the same joint phase model as the woody load panels, retaining its pre/post covariance. - Retain the thesis visual grammar—model estimate point with a colored 95% CI range—for the six paired panels. Label pre-PCT-only litter and duff panels explicitly; do not imply a post-PCT zero or estimate. - Plot the matched woody vegetation difference separately with a zero reference line. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load, so it must not be styled as another phase estimate. - Use panel-specific y-scales and a 3 × 3 layout to keep the broad load range legible. Keep full model registries, diagnostics, and pairwise comparisons in linked artifacts rather than adding them to the figure. #### Suggested deliverables 1. A nine-panel model-estimate figure: six paired phase panels, litter, duff, and the matched woody vegetation-difference panel. 2. A publication caption and a short Results paragraph, both marked **Pending review** when draft-ready. 3. A linked table or CSV of complete phase-by-treatment model estimates and a link to the model-selection register used for the draft. #### Completed output ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![R-D04 full fuel inventory by retention treatment. #### Prediction and interpretation review {#rd04-inference-review} **Implemented approach:** use **study-standardized, population-averaged expected loads** as the baseline for mean fuel loading in comparable systems. Integrate over the fitted random-intercept distributions and include modeled zeros, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts. Retain the historical zero-random-effect predictions as a clearly labeled reference/sensitivity summary in the audit. R-D04 now uses this integrated interpretation throughout, with woody mean change derived from the joint phase model; the fitted load models remain provisional pending scientific review. The original generator has been retired in favor of `08-generate-rd04-integrated-figure.R`. ##### What the prediction arguments actually do | Calculation | Quantity estimated | Appropriate interpretation | |---|---|---| | `re.form = NULL` with known grouping IDs | Expected response conditional on fitted random effects for those sites, blocks, corners, and transects | Conditions in the sampled units; average over an explicitly weighted set of these units if that is the target | | `re.form = NA` (or `~0`) | Expected response with all random effects set to zero | A reference at the center of the latent random-effect distribution | | `re.form = NULL`, with selected random-only grouping variables set to `NA` in `newdata` | Retains known-group effects for the remaining grouping variables and sets the selected groups' effects to zero | A conditional reference, e.g., a known site with zero lower-level effects | | Integrate expected responses over the fitted random-effect distribution | Arithmetic expected load for a population of exchangeable sampling units | The model-based mean-load baseline used in R-D04 | `marginaleffects` passes the random-effect arguments to the fitted model's prediction method. Its `by` argument and `avg_predictions()` average the predictions supplied to them; they do not change zero-effect predictions into random-effect-integrated predictions. This distinction follows the [mixed-model vignette](https://marginaleffects.com/bonus/lme4.html), the [prediction reference](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/predictions.html), and the distinction between observed-group averaging and new-group integration in the [Bayesian vignette](https://marginaleffects.com/bonus/brms.html#averaging-marginalizing-integrating-random-effects). For `glmmTMB`, arbitrary formulas selecting random effects in `re.form` are not supported. Selected grouping variables can instead be set to `NA`, but this is unsuitable when a variable is also required as a fixed predictor: `site`, for example, must remain defined for the post-PCT 100-hour model's zero component. `allow.new.levels = TRUE` permits new grouping IDs; it does not request integration over their possible effects. See the [model's prediction documentation](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/reference/predict.glmmTMB.html). Two different uses of “conditional” also need separating: `type = "conditional"` requests the conditional-distribution mean, whereas `re.form` controls conditioning on random effects. For these zero-inflated Gamma models, `type = "response"` returns $(1-p_0)\mu_+$, including the modeled probability of zero, while `type = "conditional"` returns $\mu_+$. Dispersion parameters affect variability and estimation but are not additional multipliers of this response mean. Gamma sampling variability should not receive a lognormal residual-variance correction. ##### Alignment of the thesis code and interpretation The controlling Results function is `marginaleffects_to_emmeans()` in `analysis/thesis/results.qmd`: **both predictions and comparisons use `re.form = NA`**. For fuel loads, its pre- and post-PCT calls use `tidyr::expand(data, treatment, site)`, giving equal site weights. Passing the predictions and pairwise-difference standard errors into `emmeans::emmobj()` changes their representation, not their underlying estimand. The earlier `re.form = NULL` exploratory basal-area plots in `regen_visualize.qmd` are not the calls controlling the thesis Results. | Thesis statement or presentation | Assessment | |---|---| | Methods: predictions incorporate all components and average over random effects to obtain population means | Partly aligned: response predictions can include the zero component, but the wrapper sets random effects to zero before averaging. The random effects were not integrated out. | | Methods: estimates apply to equal proportions of similar sites, specifically north- and south-facing aspects | Equal site weights are explicit for fuel grids. Zeroing site random effects does not reproduce an aspect mixture on a nonlinear response scale; aspect was not a fixed adjustment variable. Transport requires an exchangeability assumption beyond the prediction settings. | | Fuel Results: “expected value” and “estimated marginal means” | Valid if identified as site-standardized expectations **at zero random effects**. Too broad if read as arithmetic population-average loads across forest heterogeneity. | | Discussion: compare “average” loads with other forest studies | State whether each value is an observed mean, a zero-effect reference, or an integrated model mean, and check component definitions and sampling protocols. These quantities are not interchangeable. | | Post-PCT caption: vegetation difference “represents slash fuels recruited to the forest floor” | Overstates the measurement: standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential contribution, not measured slash deposition. R-D04's qualified caption is better aligned. | | Results: pre/post estimates are not statistically comparable because model structures differ | Different structures alone do not prevent comparison. Formal phase differences need an explicit common estimand and their covariance, accounting for pairing. Separate phase CIs do not supply a paired change test. | | Discussion/conclusions: PCT “resulted in” or “generated” the observed dead-fuel changes | The observed transition supports association; attributing all change to PCT requires the design/time assumptions. No unthinned contemporaneous comparison is used by these predictions. | The same wrapper controls regeneration and sprout Results. Basal area, Douglas-fir counts, and year-10 height use nonlinear links, so zero-effect and integrated means can differ there too. Height increment uses an identity link; integration over mean-zero random effects leaves its expected value unchanged, for a fixed covariate distribution. The Results grids also vary: treatment height-increment summaries explicitly balance years, whereas the by-year analysis uses `newdata = NULL` and averages within observed species/year cells. Those are different standardization choices and should be described separately. The fuel integration code below is deliberately restricted to its audited model structures; it is not a general-purpose replacement for those other analyses. One numerical provenance issue also deserves attention: the Discussion reports about **42 Mg/ha** of pre-PCT 1,000-hour fuel. Reproducing the Results wrapper on the saved thesis models gives an equal-treatment reference mean of **32.63 Mg/ha**. The Discussion value may be an observed summary, but it should not be presented as the grand mean of these particular model predictions without a separate source. The audit preserves all reproduced thesis fuel estimates. ##### How R-D04 compares with the thesis The original R-D04 and thesis fuel Results used the **same zero-random-effect target** and equal-site weighting. Both used valid prediction grids: the thesis expanded the observed treatment and site levels, and R-D04 retained observed rows with valid nested identifiers, one per site/treatment/phase. Neither approach introduced a grid discrepancy for these zero-effect predictions. The updated R-D04 retains equal-site weighting and integrates over random effects. Every phase-specific mean averages four site contexts; post-PCT 100-hour fuel additionally retains fixed site effects in its zero component. Numerical changes from the thesis to the original R-D04 arose from revised fitted models and component definitions, not a switch from `marginaleffects` to custom prediction. The updated figure also changes the estimand by integrating over random effects. The directly comparable deadwood example below separates these changes. Thus, with $v=\sum_k\sigma_k^2$ across **all** modeled random-intercept levels, $$ M_{th}=\exp(v/2)\, \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}(1-p_{0,sth})\exp(x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta). $$ This is exact under the fitted model, not a generic bias-correction option. The same multiplier across treatments within a fitted load model preserves ratios and rankings, while changing absolute loads and differences. Inference must still propagate uncertainty in the multiplier; old p-values and standard errors should not simply be carried over. The separate Student-t difference model was replaced in the display by the integrated joint phase-model contrast so that woody change equals the difference between the displayed arithmetic mean loads. Its uncertainty retains the joint pre/post covariance, keeping the change estimate consistent with the matched design and the mean-load interpretation of the other panels. For post-PCT 100-hour fuel, “site-standardized” specifically retains an equal mixture of the **four fitted zero-process site contexts**. Integration of the random intercepts cannot create a zero-process coefficient for a fifth site. The baseline therefore concerns comparable contexts, not a fitted prediction for any arbitrary new forest. Four sites also provide limited information about the site-variance distribution. A regional mean, or an explicitly 50:50 aspect-standardized mean, would need a justified target distribution and sufficient covariate information to support that standardization. The demonstration holds fitted load models fixed and changes the estimand; woody change now uses their joint phase model. Selected GS examples below show why the distinction matters (Mg/ha). The intervals describe uncertainty in the integrated **mean**, not variation in a new forest or transect. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Component |Phase | Zero-effect reference| Integrated mean| 95% lower| 95% upper| |:---------------------|:-------|---------------------:|---------------:|---------:|---------:| |100-hour |postpct | 16.68| 19.64| 11.77| 32.78| |Herbaceous vegetation |prepct | 0.22| 0.51| 0.20| 1.28| |Herbaceous vegetation |postpct | 0.09| 0.18| 0.05| 0.59| |Woody vegetation |prepct | 30.03| 39.90| 21.32| 74.67| |Woody vegetation |postpct | 1.85| 2.46| 1.29| 4.68| ::: ::: The implementation in `07-audit-rd04-inference.R` demonstrates both routes: 1. **Historical reference target:** `marginaleffects::avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, by = ..., type = "response", re.form = NA)` agrees with `predict()` followed by explicit matrix averaging. The custom variance is `A %*% prediction$cov.fit %*% t(A)`. 2. **Implemented integrated target:** a nonlinear functional supplied to `marginaleffects::hypotheses()` averages the response means after analytic integration. A separate custom implementation derives its gradient and calculates `G %*% V %*% t(G)`. Both use the full covariance of the fitted nonrandom parameters, including zero-model coefficients, log random-effect standard deviations, and their cross-covariances. Merely multiplying an `avg_predictions()` interval by `exp(v/2)` would omit uncertainty in $v$. The [hypotheses documentation](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/hypotheses.html) supports nonlinear functionals and supplied covariance matrices. Here the full parameter table is supplied explicitly because ordinary fixed-coefficient prediction covariance alone does not include the integration multiplier's variance. These are asymptotic delta-method intervals, conditional on the chosen models and the reference grid. They do not include model-selection or fuel-component-derivation uncertainty. Refitted parametric bootstrap intervals are a useful final sensitivity check, particularly for herbaceous loads with large variance corrections and only four sites. **Verification:** the audit checks all 60 historical comparison cells for agreement of reference point estimates and SEs, integrated point estimates, and integrated SEs; the latter agree within a relative/absolute tolerance of $10^{-4}$. It checks the integration multiplier against numerical quadrature, the matrix predictions against `predict.glmmTMB()`, and the retired script's checksum before and after the run. It additionally verifies all four woody mean contrasts with cross-phase covariance and reproduces the 48 thesis fuel reference estimates. Outputs and the R/package session record are in `analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/inference-audit/`.

##### Methods wording For the implemented population-average baseline: > We estimated treatment- and phase-specific mean fuel loads by averaging > response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally > weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating > over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates > provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% > confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full > parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. The matched-contrast qualification can be stated in its own Methods sentence: > Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus > post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint > covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.
